analysis.one_liner: Bans government agencies from buying Americans' location, browsing, and subscriber records from data brokers without a warrant.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee in the 117th Congress, ending with one cosponsor and no vote of any kind.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would stop law enforcement and intelligence agencies from getting around the warrant requirement by buying Americans' records — phone location data, web browsing and search history, subscriber information — from data brokers and other third parties. It would make such purchased records inadmissible as evidence, require a court order on the strictest applicable standard before the government could compel a third party to hand them over, and make the foreign-intelligence surveillance courts the only legal channel for collecting Americans' location and browsing data.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose movements, online activity, and account records would no longer be obtainable by federal agencies simply by paying a broker. Anyone whose location history could reveal visits to a clinic, a place of worship, a protest, or an attorney's office would gain a legal shield: agencies would need a court order, and data bought in violation of the ban could not be used against anyone in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone with a phone or online account

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits law enforcement agencies and intelligence agencies from obtaining covered customer or subscriber records, or information obtained illegitimately, from a third party in exchange for anything of value — closing the loophole where agencies buy data they could not legally compel.

Makes records or information obtained in violation of the ban, and any evidence derived from them, inadmissible in any trial, hearing, or other proceeding at any level of government, so the rule has teeth rather than being advisory.

Requires a court order — applying the most stringent standard under federal statute or the Constitution — before a government entity can compel a third party to disclose a covered record, putting broker-held data on the same footing as data held directly by phone and internet providers.

Makes the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act the exclusive means by which location information, web browsing history, and internet search history of people in the United States can be collected for foreign intelligence purposes, ending warrantless end-runs around the surveillance courts.

Bars intermediary service providers — companies that deliver, store, or process communications on behalf of providers — from knowingly divulging the contents of stored communications or subscriber records to the government.
Directs the Attorney General to adopt minimization procedures to limit the acquisition, retention, and dissemination of any information agencies acquire in violation of the ban.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers and the companies that sell location, browsing, and subscriber records lose the government as a customer, and federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies lose a fast, warrantless route to Americans' personal data. Taxpayers bear little direct cost; the burden is slower investigations where a warrant or court order is now required.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers selling to government agencies

drawbacks.text: Requiring court orders before obtaining third-party records adds time and friction to investigations; agencies argue that speed sometimes matters in criminal and counterintelligence work, and the bill would force them through the same judicial process as a warrant application.

The definition of 'illegitimately obtained information' leans on private companies' own service agreements and privacy policies, so the level of protection a person gets would depend on the fine print of a contract they never negotiated with the broker that sold them out.

The exclusion of illegally purchased records from evidence would, in some cases, cost prosecutors usable evidence in real criminal cases — a deliberate deterrent, but a real one an honest supporter has to acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and structural: a warrant or court order before the government can buy a person's movements, browsing history, or account records, with a penalty (exclusion) that gives agencies a reason to comply. The costs are comparatively narrow — some investigative delay and lost revenue for brokers — and the bill preserves emergency pathways through the existing wiretap statute. The main design weakness is anchoring 'illegitimately obtained' in private terms of service, which makes protection uneven. On balance a well-targeted privacy protection, and its death means none of these limits exist in law.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Judiciary and Intelligence committees for the rest of the two-year Congress — referred to a subcommittee in October 2021 — and never got a markup or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler introduced the bill on April 21, 2021, with Rep. Zoe Lofgren co-introducing; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and, in addition, to the Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
On October 19, 2021, the House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee's Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — the last action ever taken on it.
Neither committee ever held a markup or reported the bill, and it attracted only one cosponsor; the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers that sell Americans' location and browsing records, and the federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies that buy them, are better off: the warrant requirement and the evidence ban were never enacted, so both can keep operating as before.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers and the agencies that buy from them

sides.party_line_note: Only House Democrats ever attached their names — the sponsor and one cosponsor — and because no committee or floor vote ever occurred, no partisan voting pattern exists to judge.

industries.note: Government agencies are a paying market for brokered location, browsing, and subscriber records; the bill bans agencies from buying those records, wiping out that line of business. Its whole purpose is to stop brokers from standing between Americans and the warrant requirement.

industries.industry: Federal law enforcement and intelligence agencies
industries.note: The bill takes away the shortcut of purchasing data — including location, browsing, and search history — that agencies could not obtain directly without a court order, and makes anything bought in violation unusable in court. Nothing in the record shows agencies fighting the bill; it died from inaction, not opposition votes.

The bill adds new restrictions on intermediary providers divulging communications content or subscriber records, and requires court orders before the government can compel third-party disclosure. Clearer legal lines generally favor both the companies and their customers' privacy, though it removes some flexibility in voluntary cooperation with agencies.
